## Task: Identify and share element-independent FEM assembly operations

Compare the verified spring and axial-bar implementations. Identify the assembly
operations that are sufficiently independent of the element formulation to
justify a shared implementation, while keeping the element-specific finite
element formulation visible.
:::

The spring and axial-bar analyses are already verified. S06 changes only their
organization: compare the visible repeated work, share the assembly operations
that have earned an abstraction boundary, and use the existing regression suite
to confirm that the accepted numerical behavior remains unchanged.

## Start from the verified baseline

Before refactoring, run the regression tests:

```text
julia test/runtests.jl
```

All existing tests should pass before you continue. This checkpoint makes the
refactoring safe to assess: the mathematical problems and accepted numerical
behavior must remain unchanged as the code organization changes.

The aim is not to eliminate every repeated line. Compare the two verified
formulations to identify FEM operations that are stable and sufficiently
independent of the element formulation to justify a shared implementation:

```text
two_springs_fem.jl
    spring-specific element formulation and analysis

axial_bar_fem.jl
    two-node axial-bar formulation and analysis

test/runtests.jl
    regression tests protecting both analyses
```

## Compare the S05 element loops

Before making any changes, compare the S05 spring and axial-bar element loops.
The code snippets below are sufficient to identify what is common and what
remains element-specific; there is no need to compare the complete files line by
line.

The essential part of the spring loop is:

```julia
k_e = element_stiffness[e]
K_e = spring_stiffness(k_e)
dof_map = [element_connectivity[e, 1], element_connectivity[e, 2]]

for i in 1:2
    I = dof_map[i]
    for j in 1:2
        J = dof_map[j]
        K[I, J] += K_e[i, j]
    end
end
```

The axial-bar loop performs additional element-specific operations and assembles
both a matrix and a consistent element load vector:

```julia
x_e = node_coordinates[element_nodes]
E_e = element_E[e]
A_e = element_A[e]
q_e = element_q[e]

L_e = x_e[2] - x_e[1]
K_e = bar_stiffness(E_e, A_e, L_e)
f_e = bar_distributed_load(q_e, L_e)
dof_map = [element_connectivity[e, 1], element_connectivity[e, 2]]

for i in 1:2
    I = dof_map[i]
    f[I] += f_e[i]
    for j in 1:2
        J = dof_map[j]
        K[I, J] += K_e[i, j]
    end
end
```

Before continuing, classify the following operations. For each one, ask whether
it depends on a particular element formulation, whether the operation itself is
element-independent, and whether the current examples provide enough evidence to
justify sharing its implementation in S06.

  | operation                                     | depends on the element formulation? | element-independent operation? | enough evidence to share in S06? |
  | --------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------: | :----------------------------: | :------------------------------: |
  | obtain $k_e$                                  |                                     |                                |                                  |
  | obtain $E_e$, $A_e$, and $q_e$; compute $L_e$ |                                     |                                |                                  |
  | construct $\mathbf K_e$ or $\mathbf f_e$      |                                     |                                |                                  |
  | construct `dof_map`                           |                                     |                                |                                  |
  | scatter $\mathbf K_e$ into $\mathbf K$        |                                     |                                |                                  |
  | scatter $\mathbf f_e$ into $\mathbf f$        |                                     |                                |                                  |

Use the table to decide whether an operation should remain specific to an
element formulation or whether it is sufficiently independent and established to
justify a shared implementation. In particular, do not decide from similar
syntax alone. Consider whether the operation represents the same conceptual task
and serves the same [abstraction](../glossary.qmd#gls-abstraction).

## Decide what should be shared

Use the comparison to examine the operations according to the three categories
described below: element-specific operations, assembly operations that are
appropriate to share, and operations that only appear similar. Before extracting
the first shared operation, make sure that the distinction between these
categories is clear.

**Element-specific operations** remain in the source file associated with each
element formulation. For the spring analysis, these are the spring stiffness
calculation and the spring element loop. For the axial-bar analysis, they are
`bar_stiffness`, `bar_distributed_load`, the axial-bar element loop, and
`recover_axial_bar_response`. These operations depend on the particular element
formulation and therefore change when that formulation changes. The axial-bar
element loop, for example, must obtain the element coordinates, material
properties, cross-sectional area, and distributed load before it can construct
the local stiffness matrix and load vector.

**Shared assembly operations** are sufficiently independent of the element
formulation to justify a common implementation. The local-to-global **matrix**
scatter-add operation is clearly repeated in both analyses. Adding forces that
are already specified at global DOFs is also common to both, although S05
implements this operation differently in the spring and axial-bar files. These
two cases therefore provide direct evidence for shared functions.

Element-vector scatter-add is different. It currently appears only in the
axial-bar analysis because the spring example has no element load vector.
Nevertheless, it is naturally part of the same small assembly layer: it is the
vector form of the same local-to-global scatter operation, its responsibility is
independent of the element formulation, and it requires only `f`, `f_e`, and
`dof_map`. Keeping matrix and vector assembly as separate functions also
preserves the distinction between the different mathematical objects being
assembled.

In each case, once the element formulation has produced a local matrix
$\mathbf K_e$, a local vector $\mathbf f_e$ when required, and the corresponding
local-to-global DOF map, the assembly operation no longer needs to know how
those quantities were obtained.

Constructing `dof_map`, however, remains visible in each element loop. Although
the spring and axial-bar examples currently construct it in a similar way, both
have only one DOF per node. In more general finite element models, the DOF map
depends on the element topology and on the number and arrangement of DOFs at
each node. S06 therefore does not yet introduce a shared DOF-map construction
function.

This illustrates an important aspect of the [Don't Repeat Yourself
(DRY)](../glossary.qmd#gls-dry) principle: similar-looking code should not be
shared automatically; the repeated code must also represent the same stable
responsibility.

**Superficially similar operations** may share syntax without having the same
responsibility. The matrix and vector scatter loops share an outer loop and a
DOF map, but they assemble different mathematical objects. This distinction will
matter when deciding whether matrix and vector assembly should remain separate
shared operations.

The separation between element-specific formulation and shared assembly follows
the finite element algorithm itself:

```text
element-specific formulation
        ↓
local K_e and possibly f_e
        ↓
element-independent assembly
        ↓
global K and f
```

The element-specific part constructs the local contributions required by the
chosen element formulation. Once those local quantities and their DOF map are
known, assembly performs the same local-to-global scatter operation regardless
of whether they came from a spring or an axial-bar element.

## First guided implementation: matrix assembly

Create `examples/fem_assembly.jl` and begin with this interface:

```julia
assemble_matrix!(K, K_e, dof_map)
```

For local DOFs $i$ and $j$, let $I$ and $J$ denote the corresponding global DOFs
obtained from the local-to-global DOF map:

$$
  I = \texttt{dof\_map}[i],
  \qquad
  J = \texttt{dof\_map}[j].
$$

Matrix assembly then performs the scatter-add operation

$$
  K_{IJ} \mathrel{+}= K^e_{ij}.
$$

Implement it by following this procedure:

1. use `axes(K_e, 1)` to iterate over the local rows of $\mathbf K_e$;
2. map local row $i$ to global row $I$ through `dof_map`;
3. use `axes(K_e, 2)` to iterate over the local columns of $\mathbf K_e$;
4. map local column $j$ to global column $J$; and
5. scatter-add `K_e[i, j]` into `K[I, J]`.

The use of `axes` follows the Julia iteration tools introduced in
@sec-julia-essentials. In S05, both element loops used fixed `1:2` ranges
because the spring and axial-bar elements each had two local displacement DOFs.
The shared matrix assembly operation should no longer encode that assumption. By
deriving the loop ranges from `K_e`, the operation is not tied to a local matrix
with exactly two rows and two columns.

This does not make the element formulations themselves generic. The appropriate
element matrix `K_e` and local-to-global `dof_map` must still be supplied; only
the scatter-add operation is being shared.

After completing the task, compare your function with this short reference
excerpt:

```julia
function assemble_matrix!(K, K_e, dof_map)
    for i in axes(K_e, 1)
        I = dof_map[i]

        for j in axes(K_e, 2)
            J = dof_map[j]
            K[I, J] += K_e[i, j]
        end
    end
end
```

The explicit loops are deliberately retained so that the local-to-global
assembly operation remains visible in the code.

## Decide where the shared file is loaded

Before modifying either source file, first make the new matrix assembly function
available to both implementations. Should `fem_assembly.jl` be included directly
inside `two_springs_fem.jl` and `axial_bar_fem.jl`, or should it instead be
included by the scripts and tests that use those files?

S06 keeps the file dependencies explicit. In the spring executable, load:

```julia
include("fem_assembly.jl")
include("two_springs_fem.jl")
```

In the axial-bar executable, load:

```julia
include("fem_assembly.jl")
include("axial_bar_fem.jl")
```

In `test/runtests.jl`, include `fem_assembly.jl` once before loading
`two_springs_fem.jl` and `axial_bar_fem.jl`. Neither source file includes
`fem_assembly.jl` itself, so the shared definitions are loaded only once in the
same test process.

## Refactor the spring implementation first

Use the new matrix function in `two_springs_fem.jl` before changing the bar
implementation. Rename `assemble_stiffness!` to `assemble_springs!`. Retain the
spring element loop, `spring_stiffness`, and construction of `dof_map`; replace
only the nested local-to-global matrix scatter with:

```julia
assemble_matrix!(K, K_e, dof_map)
```

Do not change the homogeneous boundary-condition treatment, the strain-energy
calculation, or the `solve_two_springs` return interface. Then run:

```text
julia test/runtests.jl
```

At this intermediate checkpoint, all six existing regression checks must still
pass.

Compare the information required by `assemble_springs!` and `assemble_matrix!`.
The spring function must know the spring stiffnesses and element connectivity,
and it must use the spring-element formulation to construct each local matrix
`K_e` and its `dof_map`. The shared matrix assembly function does not need any
of this spring-specific information: it receives `K_e` and `dof_map` and only
scatters the local matrix into the global matrix.

The two functions therefore have different responsibilities: `assemble_springs!`
forms the element contribution, while `assemble_matrix!` assembles that
contribution into the global system.

## Second guided implementation: vector assembly

Now turn to the axial-bar formulation. Add this second interface to
`fem_assembly.jl`:

```julia
assemble_vector!(f, f_e, dof_map)
```

For local DOF $i$, let $I$ denote the corresponding global DOF,

$$
  I = \texttt{dof\_map}[i].
$$

Vector assembly then performs

$$
  f_I \mathrel{+}= f^e_i.
$$

Write the function by using `axes(f_e, 1)` to iterate over the local entries of
$\mathbf f_e$, mapping local index $i$ to global index $I$, and scatter-adding
`f_e[i]` into `f[I]`. As in the matrix assembly function, deriving the iteration
range from the supplied local quantity avoids encoding the two-DOF assumption.
Only after implementing the function, compare it with this reference excerpt:

```julia
function assemble_vector!(f, f_e, dof_map)
    for i in axes(f_e, 1)
        I = dof_map[i]
        f[I] += f_e[i]
    end
end
```

In `assemble_axial_bar!`, retain the element loop; extraction of nodes,
coordinates, $E_e$, $A_e$, and $q_e$; computation of $L_e$; construction of
$\mathbf K_e$ and $\mathbf f_e$; and construction of `dof_map`. Replace only the
scatter operations with:

```julia
assemble_matrix!(K, K_e, dof_map)
assemble_vector!(f, f_e, dof_map)
```

Run the regression suite again. The existing references must remain unchanged.

## Why not combine matrix and vector assembly?

The former axial-bar scatter loop placed vector assembly inside the outer matrix
loop:

```julia
for i in 1:2
    I = dof_map[i]
    f[I] += f_e[i]

    for j in 1:2
        J = dof_map[j]
        K[I, J] += K_e[i, j]
    end
end
```

Since the two operations use the same `dof_map` and share the outer loop, why
not extract them as one function?

Before answering, consider these questions:

- Does every element that contributes a matrix necessarily contribute a vector?
- Can matrix and vector assembly occur independently?
- Is sharing control-flow structure the same as sharing a responsibility?

The answer distinguishes *syntactic similarity* from *conceptual
responsibility*. Matrix assembly and vector assembly are distinct finite element
operations. An analysis may assemble a stiffness matrix without an element load
vector, or it may assemble a vector independently of a matrix. Sharing part of
their control flow is not sufficient reason to give them one responsibility.

Similar code does not necessarily represent the same abstraction. A future
higher-level operation could compose `assemble_matrix!` and `assemble_vector!`
if a genuine repeated need for that composition emerges. For now, keeping them
separate helps make clear that matrix assembly and vector assembly act on
different mathematical objects and have different responsibilities. S06
therefore avoids combining them simply because parts of their code look similar.

## Third guided implementation: nodal loads

Compare the two existing ways of adding forces that are already specified at
global DOFs. At the S05 starting state, the spring implementation encapsulates
the operation in:

```julia
assemble_forces!(f, applied_forces)
```

The axial-bar solver instead contains the equivalent explicit loop:

```julia
for (dof, value) in applied_forces
    f[dof] += value
end
```

Both forms add the same kind of force to the global vector. Before naming a new
function, decide whether this is the same operation as assembling an element
vector:

```text
assemble_vector!
    local element vector
    → requires a local-to-global map
    → global vector

add_nodal_forces!
    force already specified at a global DOF
    → no element map is required
    → global vector
```

An element vector is local and needs a DOF map. A nodal force is already
specified at a global DOF. They are different FEM operations.

Add the interface

```julia
add_nodal_forces!(f, applied_forces)
```

to `fem_assembly.jl`. Iterate through the supplied `(dof, value)` pairs and add
each value to `f[dof]`. The name describes the operation precisely and
distinguishes it from element-vector assembly. Remove the spring-specific
`assemble_forces!` definition, replace its call with `add_nodal_forces!`, and
replace the equivalent explicit loop in the axial-bar solver with the same
shared function. Then run the regression suite again. The same six regression
checks must pass.

This builds on the distinction introduced in
@sec-four-element-axial-bar-analysis between distributed element loads and
concentrated nodal loads. The former produce element load vectors that must be
assembled, while the latter are already defined at global DOFs and can be added
directly to the global load vector.

## Inspect the result

After completing the three refactoring steps and checking each one with the
regression tests, compare your implementation with the expected result shown
next.

The refactored spring element loop should have the following structure:

```julia
K_e = spring_stiffness(k_e)
# construct dof_map for this spring element
assemble_matrix!(K, K_e, dof_map)
```

Similarly, the refactored axial-bar element loop should retain the
formulation-specific quantities while delegating the shared assembly operations:

```julia
K_e = bar_stiffness(E_e, A_e, L_e)
f_e = bar_distributed_load(q_e, L_e)
# construct dof_map for this bar element
assemble_matrix!(K, K_e, dof_map)
assemble_vector!(f, f_e, dof_map)
```

The two element loops are therefore still different, as expected. Each retains
the operations required by its own element formulation, while the
local-to-global assembly steps have been moved to the shared functions.

## Reflect on the programming principles

The S06 refactoring can now be interpreted in terms of several programming
principles. The concepts introduced below provide a vocabulary for understanding
why the code was organized in this way; they are design principles rather than
rigid rules that require every implementation to have the same structure.

The first of these principles is [separation of
concerns](../glossary.qmd#gls-separation-of-concerns). Element formulation and
local-to-global assembly perform different parts of the finite element
algorithm, so S06 keeps them separate. This separation can then be examined more
closely through several related principles: the Single Responsibility Principle,
cohesion, coupling and interface design, and a restrained application of DRY.
Each of these is discussed in the following subsections.

### Single Responsibility Principle

The distinction between element formulation and local-to-global assembly also
illustrates the [Single Responsibility
Principle](../glossary.qmd#gls-single-responsibility-principle): a function
should have a coherent responsibility and a principal reason to change. It does
not mean that a function should merely "do one tiny thing." Element formulation
changes for spring- or bar-specific reasons, while local-to-global scatter-add
assembly changes for assembly-algorithm reasons.

The principle does not require fragmenting every sequence of formulas. For
example, `recover_axial_bar_response` computes displacement increments, strains,
stresses, and axial forces. Together these form one coherent two-node axial-bar
response-recovery responsibility. Splitting them solely because several formulas
appear inside the function would make the calculation harder to follow.

### Cohesion

The three functions in `fem_assembly.jl` form a small, cohesive family: each
operates on contributions that must be added to global finite element arrays.
This [cohesion](../glossary.qmd#gls-cohesion) gives the file a clear purpose. A
more generic `fem_utils.jl` file would make that purpose less clear and could
gradually collect unrelated operations.

### Coupling and interface design

The interface

```julia
assemble_matrix!(K, K_e, dof_map)
```

does not need to know the spring stiffness, Young's modulus, cross-sectional
area, coordinates, distributed load, or element type. A useful function
interface is defined partly by what the function does *not* need to know. This
reduces [coupling](../glossary.qmd#gls-coupling) between element formulation and
assembly: each element formulation provides the required local data, while the
assembly function is concerned only with the scatter-add operation.

### Don't Repeat Yourself without dogmatism

The [Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY)](../glossary.qmd#gls-dry) principle is useful
when repeated code performs the same stable operation. It should not be applied
mechanically simply to remove every instance of repeated code.

MiniFEM intentionally retained duplicated matrix scatter code through the
earlier snapshots. The operation first needed to remain visible alongside the
element formulations that required it. Refactoring becomes appropriate at this
stage because matrix scatter is now repeated, stable, already understood, and
independent of the particular spring or bar formulation. Keeping separate copies
would therefore begin to distract from the differences that actually matter
between the two element formulations.

The vector scatter operation is not yet repeated across the two examples, but it
has the same element-independent local-to-global assembly role for a different
mathematical object. Keeping matrix and vector assembly as separate functions
also shows an important limit to DRY: similar syntax alone is not sufficient
reason to combine operations when they have different responsibilities.

## What S06 deliberately does not refactor

S06 is also useful for identifying which parts of the two implementations are
*not* ready to be shared:

- boundary-condition treatment;
- spring and axial-bar element formulations;
- axial-bar response recovery;
- strain-energy computation;
- reaction recovery; and
- solver structure.

Some of these operations are genuinely different and should remain separate;
others have not yet appeared often enough, or in a sufficiently stable form, to
justify a shared abstraction. Whether any of them should be shared later will
depend on evidence from future examples.

The boundary-condition treatment is a clear example. The spring analysis uses
homogeneous row-and-column modification, whereas the axial-bar analysis uses
free/constrained partitioning and can therefore accommodate nonzero prescribed
displacements. These are different implementations introduced for different
stages of the course, so S06 leaves both visible rather than forcing them into a
shared function prematurely.

The same reasoning applies to the other items in the list. Some may remain
specific to their current formulations, while others may become candidates for
later refactoring if future examples reveal a stable common operation. S06
therefore shares only those operations for which a stable element-independent
responsibility is already sufficiently clear.

## Final regression checkpoint

The regression references introduced in S04 and extended in S05 are unchanged.
After completing the refactoring, run:

```text
julia test/runtests.jl
```

The expected result is:

```text
Two-spring regression tests: 4 pass
Four-element axial-bar regression tests: 2 pass
```

If so, the tests confirm that the accepted numerical results remain unchanged
after the refactoring.

## What comes next

S06 has introduced the first shared MiniFEM assembly operations. The
element-specific FEM calculations remain visible, and the current source still
shows which responsibilities have not yet earned a shared abstraction.

Attention now shifts from code organization back to element formulation. The
following theory chapters develop the coordinate transformations and
Gauss--Legendre quadrature needed to evaluate element integrals numerically. A
later coding task will then adapt the verified axial-bar implementation by
adding a quadrature-based route alongside its existing closed-form evaluation.
